Saturday nights in our village brought a lovely feeling of putting things in order and enjoying a quiet pause before beginning life afresh. That feeling encouraged Joe to risk staying out half an hour later than on other nights. When both the half hour and his rum and water were finished, he stood up to leave and took my hand.

"Wait just a moment, Mr. Gargery," the stranger said. "I think I've a shiny new shilling somewhere in my pocket. If I have, the boy can have it."

He found it among a handful of small coins, wrapped it in some crumpled paper, and handed it to me. "Yours!" he said. "Remember, yours to keep."

I thanked him, staring much longer than was polite and clinging tightly to Joe. He wished Joe goodnight and said the same to Mr. Wopsle, who left with us. For me he had only a look from the eye he used for aiming—or rather, no look at all, because he shut it. But closing an eye can communicate wonders.

Had I felt like talking on the way home, I would have had to supply all the conversation. Mr. Wopsle left us outside the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe walked the entire way with his mouth wide open, trying to wash away the rum with as much fresh air as possible. But the sudden return of my old wrongdoing and my old acquaintance had left me almost stunned. I could think of nothing else.

When we arrived in the kitchen, my sister wasn't in a particularly bad mood. This unusual fact encouraged Joe to mention the shiny shilling. "A counterfeit, I'll bet," Mrs. Joe declared triumphantly. "Otherwise he wouldn't have given it to the boy! Let me see."

I unwrapped it, and it turned out to be genuine. "But what's this?" Mrs. Joe demanded, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. "Two one-pound notes?"

Indeed they were: two thick, sweaty one-pound notes that looked as though they had enjoyed the closest possible acquaintance with every cattle market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat again and ran back to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was away, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, feeling fairly certain the man would already be gone.

Before long Joe returned. The man had left, he said, but Joe had left a message at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the banknotes.

Waking that morning, Tom wondered where he could be. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and glanced about; then he understood. Dawn was cool and gray, and the woodland's profound stillness and silence carried a delightful feeling of rest and peace. No leaf moved, and no noise interrupted great Nature's contemplation. Drops of dew pearled the grass and foliage. White ash lay over the fire, from which a slender blue thread of smoke climbed directly upward. Joe and Huck remained asleep.

Far off among the trees a bird called, and another replied; soon afterward came a woodpecker's tapping. Little by little the cool, dim gray brightened, while sounds increased and living things began to stir. Before the thoughtful boy unfolded the wonder of Nature waking and setting to work. A small green worm crawled across a wet leaf, occasionally raising two-thirds of its length into the air to 'sniff about' before moving on, for it was taking measurements, Tom decided. When the creature approached him of its own accord, he remained motionless as a stone. His hopes rose whenever it advanced towards him and sank whenever it appeared to favour another direction. Finally, after an agonizing pause with its body arched in the air, it came firmly down upon his leg and began travelling across him. His heart overflowed with delight: this promised a new suit of clothes, and surely nothing less than a splendid pirate uniform. A line of ants now materialized from no particular place and attended to its business. One stout-hearted worker passed carrying a dead spider five times its own size, then hauled its burden straight up a tree. A spotted brown ladybird climbed to the dizzy summit of a grass blade. Tom stooped close and told her, 'Ladybird, ladybird, fly home away; your house is burning, your children alone.' She promptly took flight to investigate. The boy felt no surprise, having long known how readily this insect believed reports of fire; he had exploited her innocence several times. Next came a tumblebug, laboriously pushing its ball. Tom touched it to watch its legs fold against its body as it pretended to be dead. By now the birds were in full uproar. A catbird, that northern mimic, settled above Tom's head and joyfully trilled her imitations of the surrounding birds. Then a jay swept down with a piercing cry, flashing like blue fire, and perched on a twig almost within his reach. Tilting its head, it inspected the strangers with boundless curiosity. A gray squirrel and a large fox squirrel came scampering along, periodically sitting upright to examine and chatter at the boys. These wild creatures had probably never encountered a person before, and could scarcely decide whether fear was necessary.

Then the ring-master made a short speech, saying he hoped there wouldn't be any disturbance, and if the fellow promised to cause no more trouble, he could ride, provided he believed he could keep his seat. Everybody laughed and agreed, and the man climbed aboard. The instant he did, the horse started plunging and kicking and frisking about, while two circus hands clung to its bridle trying to restrain it. The drunk fellow gripped its neck, his heels shooting up with every leap, and the audience stood and hollered and laughed till their faces ran with tears. Finally, despite everything the circus men could do, the horse escaped and tore round the ring like all creation. That drunkard lay sprawled over it, clutching its neck, with one leg dangling nearly to the ground on this side and then the other on that side, and the people went wild. I couldn't see the joke; watching his danger had me shaking all over. Before long, though, he scrambled astride and caught the bridle, swaying back and forth. A moment later he sprang upright, let go of the bridle, and stood there! And the horse still racing like a house on fire. He sailed round standing up, comfortable as could be, as though he'd never tasted liquor in his life. Then he started stripping off his clothes and throwing them about. They came off so thick that the air seemed almost choked with them; he peeled away seventeen suits altogether. At last he stood there slender and handsome, wearing the showiest, prettiest outfit anybody ever saw. He laid into the horse with his whip and sent it flying; then he hopped off, bowed, and danced away to the dressing-room, with everybody roaring in delight and amazement.

Now the ring-master discovered how completely he'd been tricked, and I reckon you never saw a ring-master look so sick. The fellow was one of his own performers! He'd invented the whole prank himself and hadn't breathed a word to anybody. I felt foolish enough for having swallowed it, but I wouldn't have traded places with that ring-master for a thousand dollars. Maybe there are finer circuses somewhere; I don't know, because I've never come across one. Whatever the case, this one suited me plenty well. Whenever I find it again, it can count on getting all the business I can give it.
